posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring CRO post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain hard, then add the 'explainability is the real product' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' moment is exactly where trust breaks — and in financial services it doesn't just break quietly, it breaks in front of a regulator. The audit trail isn't a nice-to-have, it's the whole product. Most analytics tools were never designed to answer 'why' — they were designed to show you 'what'. Curious how your team is thinking about what explainability actually needs to look like before you'd let AI back into the workflow?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO venting about BI adoption failure with two more ICPs engaging — validate the real problem (trust, not tooling) and add a sharp observation without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the problem. It's that the first time a number looked wrong — even slightly — everyone quietly decided Excel was safer. Trust in data is built in moments of doubt, not moments of launch. What did your finance team actually catch that made them stop believing it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why dashboards get ignored' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is actually pretty common — I've seen ops teams with 80+, and the honest reason is nobody wanted to be the person who cut a metric and looked like they stopped caring about it. The dashboard becomes a political document instead of a decision tool. The jump to 85% usage is the real signal though — people don't ignore dashboards because they're lazy, they ignore them because the dashboard wasn't built around how they actually think. Makes you wonder how many tools get blamed for a design problem.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail engaging on self-service BI failure thread — validate the 'who owns truth' framing and add the missing layer: tools don't fail, governance does, but governance without buy-in is just more process nobody follows
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem isn't a Power BI problem, it's a 'nobody agreed on the rules before handing out the keys' problem. Most companies skip straight to the tool and never have the messy conversation about what revenue actually means — which business unit, which date, net or gross. The technology was never going to force that alignment. So the real question isn't who owns the truth, it's who had the authority to define it in the first place?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk (not just accuracy) — validate the reframe with a sharper observation, with a CEO from a data security firm watching
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and most analytics vendors are still treating it as an accuracy problem to engineer away. But the real exposure is the gap between how confident AI outputs look and how confident they actually are — a hallucinated number in a clean dashboard gets trusted faster than a shaky number in a spreadsheet. The UI is doing the security work now, and it's not built for that job. Who's actually holding vendors accountable for that gap?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm naming the exact pain Milo is built to solve, with a COO prospect in the thread — validate the observation with a sharper diagnosis, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is almost a rite of passage at this point. The dirty secret is most of these platforms were designed around the assumption that someone technical would sit between the tool and the business — 'self-service' just meant fewer developers, not actual independence. So the builder becomes the bottleneck, and the investment quietly turns into shelfware. What would it even look like if the benchmark was 'can your ops lead answer a question on a Monday morning without asking anyone'?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director flagging a classic data trust breakdown — validate the root cause (process not product), add nuance on why 'culture' alone isn't the full picture either
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter logics — that's not a culture problem, that's a governance vacuum that culture gets blamed for. The CFO asking that question is actually the healthy sign. The dangerous version is when nobody notices the numbers don't match and decisions get made anyway. Does your org have anyone who actually owns what 'the right filter' is, or is it still tribal knowledge?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with shadow AI as the punchline — validate the 12% problem with a sharper diagnosis before anyone else does
posts.draft_comment: That 12% number is doing a lot of work here. The ChatGPT-on-phones thing isn't a security problem, it's a signal — people found a tool that actually answers their question instead of waiting for them to already know the right one. Most orgs I talk to are solving the wrong half of this. Is the plan to tighten the guardrails or actually fix why Copilot feels like homework?
